paper_metadata.title: Effect of Vanadium Element on Creep Behavior and Microstructure Evolution of a High Strength Ni-Based Wrought Superalloy

evidence.quote: The influence of V contents (0.6 wt%, 0.8 wt% and 1.0 wt%) on the microstructure and creep behavior of a Nickel-based superalloy was investigated.
This study revealed a direct correlation between V content and microstructural evolution in Ni-based superalloys.

evidence.section: 4.1 Effect of V Content on the Microstructure
evidence.quote: SEM–EDS analysis was performed to quantify V concentrations in MC carbides, blocky M6C carbides, and γ matrix (Table 2).

The γ′ phase distribution displays a characteristic bimodal morphology: (1) primary γ′ precipitates (> 500 nm) predominantly located at GBs (Fig. 1d-e), and (2) secondary γ′ phases distributed throughout the grain interiors (Fig. 1f-h). Statistical measurements indicate average secondary γ′ sizes of 116 ± 10 nm, 94 ± 10 nm, and 98 ± 10 nm for the 0.6 V, 0.8 V, and 1.0 V alloys, respectively.

Statistical measurements indicate average secondary γ′ sizes of 116 ± 10 nm, 94 ± 10 nm, and 98 ± 10 nm for the 0.6 V, 0.8 V, and 1.0 V alloys, respectively.
In the 0.6 V alloy, fine M6C carbides are uniformly distributed along GBs.
The 0.8 V alloy retains this fine GB M6C distribution while also developing larger blocky M6C precipitates near MC carbides.
Notably, the 1.0 V alloy demonstrates a substantial increase in granular M6C carbide density compared to the other compositions, forming an essentially continuous GB network.
At 650 °C/1010 MPa, the microstructure exhibits an extensive network of stacking faults (SFs) intersecting along two distinct slip systems within the grains.
Additionally, a considerable number of micropores were observed along GBs in both the 0.6 V and 1.0 V alloys, with the 1.0 V alloy exhibiting a particularly high density of these defects.
Additionally, a considerable number of micropores were observed along GBs in both the 0.6 V and 1.0 V alloys, with the 1.0 V alloy exhibiting a particularly high density of these defects.

The extensive micropore formation in the 1.0 V alloy is primarily attributed to the near-continuous carbide network along GBs, which impairs coordinated deformation and promotes micropore nucleation at carbide interfaces.
As a result, the 0.8 V alloy, with its discrete M6C carbide distribution, exhibited superior creep resistance at elevated temperatures.
In contrast, at higher temperatures (750 °C/620 MPa and 800 °C/500 MPa), GB mobility was activated, making GB slip the dominant creep mechanism.
At 650 °C/1010 MPa, the 1.0 wt% V alloy, containing a high density of granular M6C carbides, demonstrated enhanced intergranular bonding strength, which contributed to prolonged creep life.

In the 0.8 V alloy, a significant amount of blocky M6C carbides precipitate near MC carbides, leading to an increased presence of large-sized carbides at the GB. These non-deformable particles can serve as potential crack initiation sites along the γ/carbide interface, further exacerbating stress concentration.

The nearly continuous distribution of M6C carbides in the 1.0 V alloy hampered the coordinated deformation ability of GBs, thereby intensifying stress concentration at these boundaries and providing additional sources for micropores.
